name: An SSH key bound to a principal acts only as that principal's actors
aliases: an actor belongs to a principal
summary: An SSH key can be bound to a principal (a LANE, lane:NAME; person:NAME is accepted too and is a different principal). ssh_forced_command.py takes --principal NAME from the authorized_keys line, never the connection, and starts the endpoint with --key-principal NAME; a line naming one twice is refused. The session registry gains an owners map, actor to principal, written only when non-empty, so an unconfigured installation keeps today's bytes and omits the principal key. On a bound key, endpoint.execute refuses every request whose actor that map does not give to the key's principal, before any action; session register with first argument register is the only exception and records the new actor under that principal; session show returns the principal when a map exists. admin.py authorized-keys --principal prints the bound line and refuses a repeated principal; authorized-keys-list marks a repeated or ill-formed principal and counts both bindings. adopt-actor gives an EXISTING actor to a principal ONCE; moving another principal's actor needs --from OWNER and is audited moved; the audit keeps the newest 200. Downgrade: an older kit refuses a registry with owners, backup included.
